before: Then there's another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don't feel your value inside, you can become a "human doer," working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism or sexual desirability, or intelligence and grades. For some people it's money or status, and for others it's a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else's problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In its controlling form, that caretaking can drift into keeping other people dependent, because being needed has become the caretaker's main source of value.
after:
### Four Pairs That Commonly Hook the Child

Pema Chödrön has a quick map for finding the bargain. It's four pairs, starting with pleasure and pain, and gain and loss. The other two are about what people think of you: praise and blame, and good reputation and disgrace. Your little one can panic when something hurts, and also when something good might disappear, like praise, romance, money, status, belonging or a spiritual high. You might still be enjoying one of those when your little one starts asking how long this is going to last.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Beauty, intelligence, achievement, and caretaking can all be real gifts. They become belonging bargains when failure in the arena feels like loss of self.

The unparented child takes those bargains because belonging feels like life or death. Self-differentiation means noticing where belonging is being purchased with self-betrayal and learning to keep your own ground. Differentiation also means noticing when praise, pity, fear, attraction, or resonance suddenly changes what you think you know.
brief:
- beauty, intelligence, achievement and caretaking can all be real gifts; they become belonging bargains when failing in the arena feels like losing yourself (keep "can all be real gifts": the gifts stay)
- the unparented child takes those bargains because belonging feels like life or death (survival, not a flaw, and not only for children of bad parents)
- self-differentiation is the name for noticing where belonging is bought with self-betrayal and keeping your own ground. The article already says both (P1 of this h2 ends "if going along means betraying yourself, that's the bargain"), so name it briefly: the rest of this h2 says "differentiation"
- it also means noticing when praise, pity, fear, attraction or resonance suddenly changes what you think you know (keep "suddenly": changing your mind isn't the alarm, and feelings can still be meaningful signals)
- context, not for the text: "become belonging bargains when…" is one case of P1's betraying-yourself line, not a second definition
length: three to five sentences, 80 to 120 words
